overview: Venezuela’s modern state separated from Gran Colombia in 1830, before this map interval. Oil, university architecture and living food traditions show different aspects of its history; political transitions and migration have reshaped communities without ending them.

periods.title: Separate republic and changing governments
periods.summary: The 1830 settlement preceded later authoritarian governments and the rise of the oil economy.

periods.title: A new political period
periods.summary: The 1958 overthrow of Pérez Jiménez opened a new electoral era.

periods.title: Constitutional change and continuing communities
periods.summary: The 1999 constitution changed the framework; later displacement extended Venezuelan communities abroad.

items.text: The 1830 Congress of Valencia adopted a constitution separating Venezuela from Gran Colombia. That event concerns the modern state’s political form. It was not the beginning of the region’s Indigenous peoples, settlement or cultural life.

Marcos Pérez Jiménez was overthrown on 23 January 1958. Diplomatic records describe the political opening that followed and the country’s dependence on oil revenues. A change of regime could alter public life while leaving major economic challenges in place.

Carlos Raúl Villanueva’s university campus in Caracas brought buildings, artworks and landscaped spaces into one design during 1940 to 1960. Reinforced concrete enabled distinctive modern forms. Education received a carefully designed setting rather than simply a collection of classrooms.

The Aula Magna incorporates Alexander Calder’s Cloud forms, and the campus also includes an Olympic Stadium and Covered Plaza. Art belongs to places where people gather and move. Its setting matters as much as the individual object.

Patios and latticed windows adapt the campus to a tropical environment. These architectural choices join modern construction with older ways of managing light and air. A building’s cleverness can lie in what it lets through as well as what it keeps out.

John Vachon’s 1944 photographs of Standard Oil operations survive at the Library of Congress. The catalog describes drilling, a refinery and workers’ children learning carpentry. This group records particular industrial settings, not a complete picture of every worker’s family life.

Cassava bread is part of Venezuelan food traditions shared with several Caribbean and Central American countries. The round breads differ in thickness, texture and flavor. One familiar food can connect communities without requiring everyone’s version to taste the same.

Knowledge of making cassava bread passes within households and communities, as well as through culinary teaching. The practice connects daily meals with Indigenous and African heritage. These are skilled food traditions, not evidence that a single recipe has remained unchanged everywhere.

In the Blessed Palm tradition, mountain journeys include storytelling and tending trails as well as gathering leaves for Holy Week. Religious observance, social memory and environmental work meet in the same activity.

Palmeros changed from cutting palms completely to pruning them, alongside new educational work involving young people. The safeguarding program shows that maintaining a tradition can require changing how it is practiced. Conservation can include learning a better way to gather.

“El idioma oficial es el castellano” means “The official language is Spanish.” This is Article 9 of the 1999 constitution in its 2009 gazette version. The same article also recognizes Indigenous languages for Indigenous peoples. Spanish writing therefore does not imply a monolingual country.

UNHCR recorded more than 7.9 million Venezuelan refugees and migrants worldwide at the end of 2024, most within Latin America and the Caribbean. Many faced barriers to housing, services and work. This dated figure records displacement; it does not mean Venezuelan communities ceased to exist.

ending.text: Venezuela continues as a state, while its communities also live across a large diaspora. The 1830 separation, 1958 regime change and 1999 constitution mark political transformations. Neither those changes nor the map’s 1878 start represent the disappearance of its peoples.
